Deepwater Investigation & Visual Analysis

DIVA

A manta-ray underwater glider that flies on buoyancy instead of propellers — and the real-time software brain we want to build it around.

01 · The problem

The ocean outlasts every battery.

75% of the seafloor is unmapped — and the vehicles we send burn most of their energy fighting drag with propellers that never stop. DIVA takes the manta ray's deal instead: make the body a wing, make moving nearly free, and let physics carry the survey.

75%ocean unmapped
0propellers in cruise

02 · How it flies

It doesn't swim. It falls — forward.

An internal ballast engine makes DIVA a few grams heavy; the hydrofoil hull converts the descent into forward glide. Purge the water and it climbs the same way. The result is a sawtooth flight path where the only continuous power draw is thinking.

Dorsal canopy

Rigid printed shell — PLA, resin or waterjet aluminum trade study.

Silicone fin skins

Dragon Skin 10/30 cast wings: compliant, sealed, replaceable.

Googly eyes ×2

Scientifically unnecessary. Emotionally essential.

Nose cameras ×2

IMX219-160 pair behind the acrylic mouth window — one forward, one down at the reef.

Ventral hull

The waterproof boundary: O-rings, gasket bead, potted passthroughs.

Jetson Nano 8 GB

Main computer — boots QNX Neutrino and hosts the vision pipeline.

BNO055 IMU

Absolute orientation, streamed straight into the pitch loop.

Bar30 depth

Pressure to 300 m at mm resolution — the glider's altimeter.

4S LiPo · 5,000 mAh

14.8 V pack behind 5 V buck and 6 V UBEC rails.

Real-time PWM I/O

PCA9685 / Nano Every — clean pulses out to every actuator.

Ballast chamber

Floods to sink, purges to climb — buoyancy is the propulsion.

NEMA 17 + TMC2209

Linear stepper meters water in and out, grams at a time, silently.

Pitchline mount

Low on the centerline: ballast position is pitch authority — and pitch is speed.

LW-25MG servos ×6

One waterproof servo per rod, hard-mounted to the chassis.

Wing spars

Each rod carries its servo's stroke out into the silicone skin.

Phased flapping

Front rod leads, rear lags — oscillation plus undulation, like the ray itself.

Hydrofoil section

Airfoil-table profile tuned for maximum lift-to-drag.

Part two

That was the hardware half.
The half you can't see is why we're writing to QNX.

The invisible half

A glider is a control loop
wearing a body.

DIVA's pitch angle is its speed, its range, its glide ratio. The loop that holds that angle has to tick on time — every time — while a vision pipeline chews camera frames beside it. That is not a job for a best-effort OS. That is a job for QNX Neutrino.

QNX use nº 1 · Architecture

Sensors in, decisions out — through a microkernel.

Resource managers wrap the IMU, depth sensor and camera as clean POSIX devices. Message passing feeds a priority-scheduled control core; actuators get their commands on schedule. Vision hangs off the side — important, never critical.

QNX use nº 2 · Determinism

Determinism you can measure in meters.

ΔX/ΔZ = cot θ — jitter in the pitch loop literally shortens the glide. QNX's priority scheduler holds the 100 Hz cadence no matter what inference is doing. On a general-purpose kernel, the same loop drifts.

QNX use nº 3 · Fault isolation

The crash that doesn't matter.

Under a microkernel, the vision pipeline is just a process in its own address space. It can die mid-dive; the process manager restarts it; the flight loop never misses a tick. On a monolithic stack, that same fault is a drowned robot.

the demo we'll run for you: kill the vision process mid-glide in the pool. DIVA keeps flying. Try that on a monolith.

Why QNX is essential — not optional

Three things only an RTOS gives this robot.

Determinism

Fixed-cadence control

Priority scheduling and priority inheritance keep the pitch loop mathematically honest — glide ratio depends on it.

Isolation

Crashes stay small

User-space drivers and a sandboxed vision pipeline: a bug costs a frame, never the vehicle.

Engineering

A teachable reference

POSIX workflow plus kernel trace data to reconcile simulation against pool telemetry.
